claim: When repairing a machine-generated Lean statement that fails to compile, regenerating the whole statement tends to find something that compiles at the cost of changing what it means, whereas repairing only the failing part preserves meaning. Supported only if, with the same formaliser and repair budget, whole-statement repair gives a higher or equal compile rate but a lower semantic-faithfulness rate than subtree-level repair on each of three benchmarks; and if, for most specialised formalisers, adding rounds of whole-statement repair lowers semantic faithfulness compared with simply sampling the same number of times.

experiments: Fix benchmarks, metrics and budget. Setup: ProverBench (high-school and introductory undergraduate), ProofNet (undergraduate) and PRIME, 156 theorems from undergraduate and graduate textbooks across algebra, analysis and number theory, formalised by hand by Lean experts. Metrics: syntax check, the share of statements that compile under Lean 4 toolchain v4.15.0, and consistency check, the share judged faithful to the natural-language statement by LeanScorer with DeepSeek-V3.2 at threshold 0.6. Because the method uses on average 2.9-3.9 model calls per problem, every method gets four calls: four samples, or one generation plus repair rounds.

Hold the formaliser fixed and change only the repair scope. Setup: the trained 7B formaliser with whole-statement repair only, four rounds, against subtree-level repair. Result: whole-statement repair compiles more often (96.00 vs 95.38, 89.76 vs 87.33, 83.97 vs 80.13 on ProverBench, ProofNet, PRIME) but is faithful less often (82.77 vs 84.00, 76.01 vs 79.51, 66.03 vs 67.95).

Check whether whole-statement repair also costs other formalisers meaning. Setup: compare each baseline's four samples with one generation plus three whole-statement repairs. Result: consistency falls for most specialised formalisers, e.g. Goedel-V2-32B 83.38 to 76.00 (ProverBench) and 66.67 to 62.82 (PRIME), Kimina-7B 65.54 to 54.46, ATF-32B 72.31 to 50.46 and 50.00 to 37.18, while compile rates change little or rise; the general model Qwen3-Max and StepFun formalisers instead gain on some benchmarks (Qwen3-Max PRIME 56.41 to 59.62).
